questions.q: How does the editorial describe the place of the intellect?
options: It is a God-given faculty for reaching conclusions – an instrument, not itself a source of knowledge – and it supports revelation
Yes. Reason and revelation are not rivals.
It is opposed to faith and must be set aside
Not quite. The article says: It is a God-given faculty for reaching conclusions – an instrument, not itself a source of knowledge – and it supports revelation.
It is useful only for worldly matters
Not quite. The article says: It is a God-given faculty for reaching conclusions – an instrument, not itself a source of knowledge – and it supports revelation.
It is the only source of all knowledge
Not quite. The article says: It is a God-given faculty for reaching conclusions – an instrument, not itself a source of knowledge – and it supports revelation.
questions.rationale: “The status of intellect is as an instrument or faculty and not that of a judge by itself… intellect, or reason, reinforces revelation and does not contradict it.”

questions.q: The physicist Paul Dirac predicted antimatter years before it was observed. What point does the article make with his example?
options: Theories should never be trusted
Not quite. The article says: Science itself accepts unseen realities inferred from sound reasoning – so belief in the unseen Hereafter is not unreasonable.
Science itself accepts unseen realities inferred from sound reasoning – so belief in the unseen Hereafter is not unreasonable
Well reasoned. Inference came first, observation later.
Only what is seen can be believed
Not quite. The article says: Science itself accepts unseen realities inferred from sound reasoning – so belief in the unseen Hereafter is not unreasonable.
Scientists often guess correctly
Not quite. The article says: Science itself accepts unseen realities inferred from sound reasoning – so belief in the unseen Hereafter is not unreasonable.
questions.rationale: “Even before these discoveries had reached the experimental stage, they were accepted as facts: they were not denied on the basis of the theoretical and abstract method of their presentation.”

questions.q: Which features of this world, according to the article, imply another world to complete it?
options: It is large, old and well mapped
Not quite. The article says: It is finite, injustice persists in it, and human potential finds no full scope here.
It is beautiful, varied and well supplied
Not quite. The article says: It is finite, injustice persists in it, and human potential finds no full scope here.
It is finite, injustice persists in it, and human potential finds no full scope here
Right. A perfect, infinite world must balance it.
It is crowded, noisy and hurried
Not quite. The article says: It is finite, injustice persists in it, and human potential finds no full scope here.
questions.rationale: “This world is finite: there must be an infinite world as well… Injustice prevails in this world: there must be a world of absolute justice.”

questions.q: Commenting on plans to make Mars habitable, what does the article say such technology, if it existed, should be used for first?
options: Restoring the Earth itself to a habitable state
Yes. And man’s true future home is Paradise.
Mining other planets
Not quite. The article says: Restoring the Earth itself to a habitable state.
Travelling to other stars
Not quite. The article says: Restoring the Earth itself to a habitable state.
Building cities on the moon
Not quite. The article says: Restoring the Earth itself to a habitable state.
questions.rationale: “If it were possible for science to make a planet in space habitable for man through new technology, then the first application of this technology should be to reshape the Earth.”

questions.q: What does the article call the basic difference between a person of faith and one without?
options: One lives as though he will stay here forever; the other knows he is on his way to the next world
Correct. Hence a sense of answerability.
One is cheerful; the other is gloomy
Not quite. The article says: One lives as though he will stay here forever; the other knows he is on his way to the next world.
One is learned; the other is not
Not quite. The article says: One lives as though he will stay here forever; the other knows he is on his way to the next world.
One is poor; the other is rich
Not quite. The article says: One lives as though he will stay here forever; the other knows he is on his way to the next world.
questions.rationale: “One without faith lives on Earth as if he is going to stay here forever, while the hallmark of true faith is the belief that one is on the way to the next world.”

questions.q: “I don’t know, is half of knowledge.” How does the article apply this saying to the seeker of God?
options: Knowledge is impossible to attain
Not quite. The article says: Admitting one’s ignorance awakens the spirit of enquiry; the more one admits it, the more one learns.
Admitting one’s ignorance awakens the spirit of enquiry; the more one admits it, the more one learns
Well read. First a seeker, then a finder.
Half of knowledge is enough
Not quite. The article says: Admitting one’s ignorance awakens the spirit of enquiry; the more one admits it, the more one learns.
One should hide what one does not know
Not quite. The article says: Admitting one’s ignorance awakens the spirit of enquiry; the more one admits it, the more one learns.
questions.rationale: “First of all, an individual has to discover his own ignorance, and then a spirit of enquiry is born within him.”

questions.q: An astronaut who had walked on the moon said he still found no peace, nor later in business and wealth. What does the article conclude?
options: Peace comes only with retirement
Not quite. The article says: Achievements cannot give inner peace; hearts find comfort in the remembrance of God.
Great achievers are never content by nature
Not quite. The article says: Achievements cannot give inner peace; hearts find comfort in the remembrance of God.
He chose the wrong professions
Not quite. The article says: Achievements cannot give inner peace; hearts find comfort in the remembrance of God.
Achievements cannot give inner peace; hearts find comfort in the remembrance of God
Right. “Something was still missing.”
questions.rationale: “I thought going to the moon would give me peace… but they didn’t… ‘Surely in the remembrance of God, hearts can find comfort.’ (13: 28)”

questions.q: One cannot expect the comforts of home in a bus or train. What does the article mean by this comparison?
options: Travel should be avoided
Not quite. The article says: This world is the journey, not the destination; full satisfaction belongs to the Hereafter.
Comfort makes people lazy
Not quite. The article says: This world is the journey, not the destination; full satisfaction belongs to the Hereafter.
This world is the journey, not the destination; full satisfaction belongs to the Hereafter
Yes. The vehicle is only a means.
Home is where one is born
Not quite. The article says: This world is the journey, not the destination; full satisfaction belongs to the Hereafter.
questions.rationale: “The vehicle is only a means of your journey, not a substitute for your home. In the same way, the fulfillment of one’s desires is simply not possible for anyone in this world.”

questions.q: What behaviour does the article describe as “seeking to deceive God”?
options: Keeping one’s good deeds secret
Not quite. The article says: Dressing up self-interest in fine words, as though one were acting for the sake of truth.
Forgetting a promise
Not quite. The article says: Dressing up self-interest in fine words, as though one were acting for the sake of truth.
Dressing up self-interest in fine words, as though one were acting for the sake of truth
Exactly. God judges by facts, not by what is said.
Praying at the wrong times
Not quite. The article says: Dressing up self-interest in fine words, as though one were acting for the sake of truth.
questions.rationale: “Their real purpose is self-interest. But they use words that conceal their true purpose, and show that they are doing so only for the sake of truth.”

questions.q: “Let every soul look to what it lays up for the future” (59:18). How does the commentary divide human life?
options: Into “today”, this world, and “tomorrow”, the Hereafter, where today’s deeds bear their result
Well read. Success lies in keeping this in mind.
Into youth and old age
Not quite. The article says: Into “today”, this world, and “tomorrow”, the Hereafter, where today’s deeds bear their result.
Into work and rest
Not quite. The article says: Into “today”, this world, and “tomorrow”, the Hereafter, where today’s deeds bear their result.
Into private and public life
Not quite. The article says: Into “today”, this world, and “tomorrow”, the Hereafter, where today’s deeds bear their result.
questions.rationale: “The present world is a man’s ‘today’ and the world of the Hereafter is man’s ‘tomorrow’. Whatever a man does in the present world, he has to face the consequences in the ensuing longer life.”
